title: Cognitive Biases in Cocaine Addiction: Evaluation of an Approach Bias Modification during Inpatient Withdrawal
summary:
Addiction often causes an imbalance in the brain: the reward system reacts extremely strongly to stimuli associated with the drug, whilst conscious control over one's own behaviour is weakened. As a result, those affected develop unconscious patterns of thought and behaviour. For example, they automatically direct their attention to the drug or feel an immediate urge to use it as soon as they see the substance. Whilst computer-assisted training programmes are already being used successfully in the treatment of alcohol dependence to modify these automatic reactions, there has been little scientific research to date for people with cocaine dependence. This project aims to fill that gap.
The main aim of the study is to investigate whether a specific computer-based training programme can help reduce the automatic urge to reach for cocaine. We are investigating whether this training reduces the strong craving for the drug and whether it helps patients remain abstinent for a longer time after discharge from hospital.
A total of 96 patients will be recruited for this study. The patients will be randomly divided into two groups. Both groups will complete the computer-based training over four consecutive days. During this, they will be shown images of cocaine and neutral images. In the training group, participants will learn to consistently "push away" the cocaine images and "pull towards" the neutral images by moving a joystick. The aim is for the brain to relearn to associate the drug with an avoidance response. In the control group, the images are moved randomly, without any specific learning effect being sought. To assess long-term success, we conduct brief telephone interviews two weeks and three months after discharge.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- diagnosed cocaine addiction
- voluntary participation
- sufficient knowledge of German
Exclusion criteria:
- use of medication to manage withdrawal symptoms
- severe traumatic brain injuries
- acute psychosis
- acute suicidal tendencies
- inadequate knowledge of German
- significant cognitive impairments
- lack of legal capacity
